title: MCP Is Not Good Yet — David Cramer, Sentry

primary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary subject is MCP as an integration protocol for connecting tools to agents, covering implementation pitfalls, OAuth, security, and response design. Sentry is a developer platform tool and the demonstrations focus on IDE coding assistant integrations via MCP in VS Code, Cursor, and Cloud Code. Cramer covers building an MCP server in two days, deploying it remotely with OAuth via Cloudflare Workers, and maintaining it with weekly updates. The content assumes familiarity with APIs, OAuth, and LLM tool calling but remains experience-based and accessible to practitioners. This is a conference presentation at AI Engineer with live demonstrations and practical advice. All ten evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript by the transcript analysis.

summary: David Cramer of Sentry presents an experience-based assessment of MCP, having built Sentry's MCP server as a side project in a couple of days. He cuts through hype—comparing it to the crypto wave—and defines MCP as simply a pluggable architecture for agents. The discussion is framed in a B2B SaaS enterprise context. Key implementation challenges emerge throughout. OAuth 2.1 is required for remote MCP but poorly supported; Sentry used a Cloudflare Shim proxy on Cloudflare Workers, also solving a websocket infrastructure gap since Sentry does not run websocket infrastructure. The biggest design insight is that MCP is not a layer over OpenAPI—exposing raw API endpoints as tools produces terrible results. Responses must be intentionally designed as markdown with bare essentials, because language models are effectively pattern matching on language, not reliably parsing JSON. Tool descriptions themselves serve as context, but token limits constrain description lengths and drive cost. Errors must also be designed as human-readable context. Cramer emphasizes cost awareness: returning too much data increases token costs and may break token limits, turning a one-dollar call into ten dollars. MCP servers are not set and forget—Sentry updates theirs weekly, tweaking and evolving. Client stability varies: VS Code Insiders is most stable, Cursor breaks frequently, Cloud Code has partial support. Cramer strongly advocates remote MCP servers with OAuth for B2B companies over standard IO, citing security risks including prompt injection. His strongest belief is that organizations should focus on building agents, treating MCP as a plug-in architecture. Sentry built an agent called Seir that performs high-quality root cause analysis, exposed through both the UI and MCP, though MCP's lack of streaming support requires polling workarounds and agents give up at some point. When this agent pattern matures through MCP, Cramer sees it as the real value unlock for B2B. He notes Sentry's MCP is fair source on GitHub. Despite everything being rough and broken, he finds MCP accessible—new vocabulary for familiar concepts—and encourages developers to try it, expecting it will stick around.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and MCP Definition
sections.summary: David Cramer introduces himself as Sentry co-founder and defines MCP simply as a pluggable architecture for agents, cutting through hype he compares to the crypto wave. He contextualizes the talk for B2B SaaS and enterprise cloud services.

sections.title: Sentry's MCP Use Case and Demo
sections.summary: Explains Sentry's motivation: they fix bugs, editors fix bugs, so bringing bug data into editors via MCP is logical. Demonstrates in VS Code Insiders where plugging in Sentry's MCP triggered about 20 API queries costing roughly $5 and began generating bug fixes.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges
sections.summary: Covers OAuth 2.1 complexity with Cloudflare Shim workaround, the critical insight that proxying OpenAPI endpoints as tools produces poor results, and varying client stability—VS Code is stable, Cursor breaks frequently, Cloud Code has partial support.

sections.title: Practical Advice: Remote MCP and Security
sections.summary: Advises B2B SaaS companies to focus on remote MCP servers with OAuth rather than standard IO. Warns strongly about security risks of standard IO including prompt injection, and advises against allowing random MCP tools or untrusted packages in organizations.

sections.title: Designing Model-Friendly Responses
sections.summary: Emphasizes that organizations must invest effort to design MCP tool responses intentionally. Sentry returns markdown with bare essentials structured for human and model reasoning, rather than raw API payloads, because if a human can reason about it, a language model can too.

sections.title: Agents, Cost Awareness, and Closing Advice
sections.summary: Continues the response design discussion: language models are pattern matching on language, not reliably parsing JSON, so use markdown. Tool descriptions, errors, and responses all serve as context for unknown agents. Cost awareness is critical—excessive tokens turn a $1 call into $10 and may hit token limits. MCP is not set and forget; Sentry updates weekly. Cramer's strongest belief is to focus on building agents, treating MCP as a plug-in architecture. Sentry built a root cause analysis agent (Seir) exposed via UI and MCP, but lack of streaming requires polling. He notes Sentry's MCP is fair source on GitHub, used Cloudflare Workers for OAuth proxy and websocket gap, and encourages developers to try MCP despite bugs, expecting it will stick around.
